subject: Critical Thinking
title: Fallacy Detection: A Practical Toolkit
description: A micro-lesson that makes Fallacy Detection: A Practical Toolkit usable.

hook.text: You don't need to memorize 100 Latin names. Three questions catch 90% of fallacies in real conversations.

buildup.text: Question 1: 'Does this evidence actually support this specific conclusion?' This catches irrelevance fallacies.

discovery.text: Question 2: 'What's being assumed but not stated?' This catches hidden premises, loaded questions, & circular reasoning.

twist.text: Question 3: 'What would change my mind?' If nothing could, your position is unfalsifiable – & you might be the fallacy.

climax.text: Apply these three questions to your own arguments first. Self-testing is more valuable than catching others' errors.

punchline.text: Three questions. Most fallacies detected. No Latin required.

quiz.question: Which question helps catch hidden assumptions in arguments?

details.summary: Fallacy detection is a trainable skill. The practical toolkit involves asking: What is the actual argument? Does the conclusion follow from the premises? Are there hidden assumptions? Is evidence being used honestly?
details.whyItMatters: A systematic approach to detecting fallacies is more reliable than memorizing a list, because new fallacies can be invented but the detection principles are universal.
takeaways: Ask for the argument's logical structure before evaluating content
Check whether the premises actually support the conclusion
Look for hidden assumptions and evaluate evidence directly

faq.question: What are the first questions to ask when evaluating any argument?
faq.answer: What is the conclusion? What are the premises? Does the conclusion follow from those premises? Are the premises true? If the answer to either of the last two questions is no, the argument fails regardless of how it feels.

faq.question: Is it better to memorize fallacy names or learn detection techniques?
faq.answer: Detection techniques are more valuable because they apply to any fallacy, including new ones. Names help communication but are secondary. Understanding why an argument fails matters more than labeling it correctly.
